rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubin describes the Book as both clear and making the truth clear, so Asad uses a compound rendering.
rows.anchor: In the consensus of authoritative opinion, both these meanings are comprised in the above instance

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari reads la'allakum ta'qilun here as an appeal to reason.
rows.anchor: This, according to Zamakhshari, is the meaning of la'allakum ta'qilun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though first addressed to the Prophet's Arabian contemporaries, these verses apply to all Arabic readers; faith must rest primarily on reason, since feeling alone is insufficient.
rows.anchor: its appeal is directed, primarily, to man's reason, and that "feeling" alone can never provide a sufficient basis of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad gives an alternate rendering of the opening phrase: by Our having revealed.
rows.anchor: By Our having revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A literal rendering of ahsan al-iqtisas is the best explanation.
rows.anchor: Lit., "with the best explanation (ahsan al-iqtisas)"

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari understands God to set forth the Qur'an in the best possible manner.
rows.anchor: the interpretation given by Zamakhshari: "We set forth this Qur'an unto thee in the best way

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says "best" concerns the manner of presentation, not the contents of Joseph's story, agreeing with Zamakhshari.
rows.anchor: According to Razi, it may safely be assumed that the adjective "best" refers not to the contents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qassa first means following step by step, then relating a story as if tracing it, and hence expounding gradually or explaining.
rows.anchor: the verb qassa (the infinitive nouns of which are qasas and igtisas) signifies, primarily, "he followed step by step"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If qasas means qissah, the verse can instead mean that God narrates the best story, namely Joseph's story.
rows.anchor: If, on the other hand, the infinitive noun qasas is regarded as synonymous, in this context, with qissah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers "We explain it in the best possible way" because it matches the opening verses' portrayal of the Qur'an as self-explanatory.
rows.anchor: the rendering "We explain it [i.e., the Qur'an] in the best possible way" is preferable

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi connects the verse's closing words with 42:52, which similarly says the Prophet did not know what revelation is or faith implies.
rows.anchor: Razi draws the reader's attention to 42:52

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad adds "of what revelation is" in brackets to clarify that parallel.
rows.anchor: hence my addition, between brackets, of the phrase "of what revelation is"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh usually marks time and means "when," but can draw attention to a sudden event or a discourse turn; Asad then renders it "lo" or "now."
rows.anchor: The particle idh is usually a time-reference, and can in most cases be translated as "when"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob understood the dream: the eleven stars symbolize Joseph's brothers, while the sun and moon symbolize his parents.
rows.anchor: the eleven stars symbolizing his brothers, and the sun and the moon his parents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike Genesis, the Qur'an shows Jacob as a prophet who immediately recognized the dream's prophetic quality and deeper implications.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an makes it clear that Jacob - who was himself a prophet - at once realized its prophetic quality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahadith literally means sayings or tidings; most commentators take it here to mean Joseph's future ability to interpret dreams.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators assume that this refers specifically to Joseph's future ability to interpret dreams

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi instead reads hadith as an event or happening, a sense Asad finds more convincing than a narrow reference to dream interpretation.
rows.anchor: Razi points out that in this context the term hadith (of which ahadith is the plural) may be synonymous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad favors Razi's event-based reading because ta'wil often means a happening's inner or final meaning rather than its outward appearance.
rows.anchor: This is, to my mind, much more convincing than a mere reference to dream-interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The min before ta'wil signals that only God has absolute knowledge of implications; prophets receive only partial insight into creation's mysteries.
rows.anchor: The use of the particle min ("of") before the term ta'wil indicates that absolute knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sa'ilin literally means those who inquire.
rows.anchor: Lit., "those who inquire"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benjamin was Joseph's full brother, both sons of Rachel; the other ten brothers were Jacob's half-brothers.
rows.anchor: Benjamin was Joseph's full brother - both being sons of Jacob's wife Rachel - whereas the other ten were only his half-brothers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means "is in most obvious error."
rows.anchor: Lit., "is in most obvious error"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's bracketed suggestion that the brothers plan to repent and resume righteousness reflects the unconscious irony recognized by most classical commentators.
rows.anchor: reflecting the unconscious irony in the attitude of Joseph's brethren - is based on the consensus of most of the classical commentators

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed plan implies that the brothers would take Joseph to a faraway land, as the preceding verse says.
rows.anchor: Sc., "and take him with them to a faraway land"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A jubb is generally a desert well cut into earth or rock without stone casing; this one was too shallow to drown Joseph but deep enough to hide him.
rows.anchor: The term jubb - rendered by me as "well" - is usually applied to a desert well simply cut through the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects God's promise that Joseph will remind his brothers of their deed with its later fulfillment in 12:89-90.
rows.anchor: See verses 89-90 of this surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Genesis calls the caravan Ishmaelites, meaning Arabs, traveling from Gilead east of the Jordan toward Egypt with spicery, balm, and myrrh.
rows.anchor: According. to the Bible (Genesis xxxvii, 25), they were "Ishmaelites" - i.e., Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bushra means "O good news!"
rows.anchor: Lit., "O good news!"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an leaves the Egyptian buyer unnamed and untitled, but al-aziz in verse 30 implies that he was a high official or nobleman.
rows.anchor: a later reference to him (in verse 30 below) as al-aziz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the verse's reference to understanding happenings' inner meanings with his explanation of ta'wil at 12:6.
rows.anchor: See note 10 above

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari says the words "and he would have succumbed" are implied in the verse.
rows.anchor: according to Zamakhshari, implied in the above sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Virtue is the inner victory over wrongful desire, not the absence of desire.
rows.anchor: the moral significance of "virtue" consists in one's inner victory over a wrongful desire, and not in the absence

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A saying transmitted by Abu Hurayrah and recorded by Bukhari and Muslim says that good intent is rewarded, while resisting a bad intent for God's sake counts as good.
rows.anchor: the well-known saying of the Prophet, recorded, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, by Bukhari and Muslim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says Joseph was among God's sincere servants.
rows.anchor: Lit., "he was among Our sincere servants"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The household witness only suggested testing the accusation by examining which way Joseph's tunic was torn.
rows.anchor: Lit., "a present one (shahid) from her household testified" - i.e., suggested a test

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic episodes in 12:26-34 are absent from Genesis, where the husband immediately believes the accusation and imprisons Joseph.
rows.anchor: the Qur'anic narrative differs from the story as told in the Bible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Almost all commentators understand "turn aside from this" as telling Joseph not to mention the matter, implying his master was ready to forgive and forget.
rows.anchor: According to almost all the commentators, the meaning is, "do not mention this to anyone"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means "we see her indeed in obvious error."
rows.anchor: Lit., "we see her indeed in obvious error"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muttaka' literally means a reclining place for eating and is used tropically for a luxurious repast.
rows.anchor: The expression muttaka'- lit., "a place where one reclines [while eating]", i.e., a "cushioned couch"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women literally deemed Joseph's beauty great.
rows.anchor: Lit., "they deemed him [i.e., his beauty] great"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means "become one of those who are humiliated."
rows.anchor: Lit., "become one of those who are humiliated"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means "the real meaning thereof."
rows.anchor: Lit., "the real meaning thereof"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph uses the opportunity to guide his fellow prisoners toward true faith, promising to interpret their dreams after a brief discourse on God's oneness.
rows.anchor: he asks them to listen first to a short discourse on the oneness of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no protection from shirk; its condemnation benefits people by freeing them from superstition and affirming their dignity as rational beings.
rows.anchor: the absolute condemnation of this sin is solely designed to benefit man by freeing him from all superstition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparative "better" means more in accord with reason's demands.
rows.anchor: better conforming to the demands of reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutafarriqan connotes plurality and separateness, here in qualities, functions, and degrees.
rows.anchor: The expression mutafarriqan connotes plurality ds well as separateness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means "names which you have named," that is, imagined figments.
rows.anchor: Lit., "names which you have named" - i.e., "figments of your own imagination"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the concluding sentence to the final sentence of 30:30.
rows.anchor: Cf. the last sentence of 30:30

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adghath literally means confusing medleys of dreams.
rows.anchor: Lit., "confusing medleys (adghath) of dreams"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self is inclined to command evil, with impulses often conflicting with the mind's moral judgment.
rows.anchor: is indeed wont to command [the doing of] evil"- i.e., is filled with impulses which often conflict

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects this weakness with Joseph's desire in 12:24 and his prayer against yielding in 12:33; those links make the statement an expression of humility, since Joseph credits God's grace for his victory.
rows.anchor: Joseph's stress on the weakness inherent in human nature is a sublime expression of humility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators read the pronoun ma as equivalent to man, meaning "he who" or "those who."
rows.anchor: According to most of the commentators, the pronoun and (lit., "that which") is here synonymous with man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph sought efficient grain reserves during the years of plenty in preparation for the following seven years of scarcity.
rows.anchor: Joseph wanted to assure an efficient build-up of grain reserves during the coming years of plenty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence makes clear that the King granted Joseph's request and that Joseph completed the work.
rows.anchor: It is obvious from the sequence that his request was granted, and that he was able to fulfil the task

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's grace may reach people in this world too, but invariably does so in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: sometimes in this world as well, but invariably in the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse literally says "for those who have attained to faith," followed by the rest of the phrase.
rows.anchor: Lit., "for those who have attained to faith..."
